Part D · Chapter 7

From language model to assistant

How a model that continues text becomes an assistant, and why it still makes things up

A pretrained model such as GPT-2 continues text, while an assistant answers questions. This chapter follows the steps between them (pretraining, instruction tuning, learning from preferences), then what a prompt can change without changing a weight, then tools and skills, and last why a fluent model makes things up. Scripted replies are labelled. The other numbers come from GPT-2 small, the Qwen2.5 tokenizer and data made up for this page.

You will need: the generation loop, sampling and loss (D3), attention (D4), the special tokens (D1) and fine-tuning (B7).

Three stages

Guess first. You type "How big does a grey bamboo shark grow?" into GPT-2, a model trained only to predict the next token. Will it answer, list more questions, or do something else?

GPT-2 is a base model: it has had pretraining and no later training. Pretraining adjusts the model's weights, the numbers inside it, to lower the loss on a very large amount of text. The loss is a score that is smaller when the actual next token gets a higher probability (the next-token chapter). So a base model continues text, and for it a question is only the start of a text. Instruction tuning trains it further on instructions paired with good replies, so its replies take the form of an answer. Preference learning then trains it on people's judgments that one reply is better than another, which moves its replies toward replies like the chosen ones.

  1. Press "Pretrained" with "Question 1": GPT-2 small, by greedy decoding (always taking the most likely token), writes 44 tokens. The reply says the shark is the size of a small car, which is false, and then repeats itself.
  2. Press "Instruction-tuned" and "Preference-tuned": these replies are scripted examples written for this page, not model output.
  3. Choose "Question 3", a made-up species: GPT-2 gives a length in meters as if the species existed, and only the preference-tuned script says it cannot find it.

Question:

One question gets a continuation from GPT-2 small, then scripted answers after instruction tuning and after preference tuning.

How it works

Follow Question 1 through the stages. Pretraining is scored only on the next token, so no part of it marks a question as a request. A question followed by a confident answer is a likely text, so GPT-2 may answer, repeat itself or write a false fact in fluent English. Instruction tuning uses replies that people wrote, or tasks rewritten as instructions, with the same next-token loss. Preference learning needs only people's comparisons of two replies, as the third section shows. The two later stages are fine-tuning (the fine-tuning chapter): small further steps on the same weights, with a risk that too much tuning makes the model lose what pretraining gave it.

Common belief. An assistant is a bigger and cleverer model than the one that predicts the next token.

Why it fails. The architecture and the generation loop stay as they were, so the assistant still writes one token at a time from a probability table. In the study of Ouyang and others (2022), labelers preferred the replies of a tuned model with 1.3 billion parameters to those of GPT-3, the base model with 175 billion.

Better account. The stages change which continuations are likely. The number of parameters limits how much of the training text the model can absorb, and tuning changes what it writes with that.

Quick quiz

Which stage needs people to write whole replies, and which needs people only to compare two replies?

Instruction tuning needs written replies (or tasks rewritten as instructions). Preference learning needs only a choice between two replies, which is quicker for the person.

Why does the pretrained model give an answer-like text at all?

Its training text contains questions followed by answers, so an answer is a likely continuation of a question. No part of its training checks whether the answer is true.

Go deeper what the research found, a debug tip about 1 min

What the research found

Wei and others (2021, the FLAN model) tuned a 137-billion-parameter model on more than 60 language tasks written as instructions. Compared with the same model before tuning, it did much better on tasks it had not seen, without examples. Ouyang and others (2022, InstructGPT) trained GPT-3 on replies written by labelers, then used human rankings of replies. On the study's prompts, the labelers preferred the replies of their 1.3-billion-parameter model to those of GPT-3 with 175 billion, more than 100 times as many parameters (175 / 1.3 is about 135). In their tests the tuned model was also more truthful, and less toxic when it was asked to be respectful, and it still made simple mistakes.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. A base model that rambles or repeats is not broken. Give it the text format it was trained on, or use the tuned version of the model. Greedy decoding also repeats a sentence once it is the most likely continuation of itself, as the first reply shows.

Instruction tuning: which tokens count

Guess first. In instruction tuning the model reads the question and the reply as one text. Should the loss count the question tokens too, or only the reply tokens?

Instruction tuning uses the next-token loss of pretraining. The loss of one token is −ln p, where p is the probability the model gave to the token that came next and ln is the natural logarithm. For example p = 0.5 gives 0.69 and p = 0.01 gives 4.6, and the unit is called a nat. What changes is the data and, usually, the loss mask, the choice of which positions add to the loss. The question tokens are read as input. In the usual setting only the reply tokens count, because the goal is a model that writes replies.

  1. The boxes are the tokens of the question and the reply, shaded by GPT-2 small's loss on them, with the loss in nats as the small number below. The reply is a shortened version of the scripted answer of the first section.
  2. Press "Instruction tuning: only the reply counts". The question tokens turn dashed, 25 tokens count, and their mean loss is 4.28 nats, a total near 107.
  3. Find the most strongly shaded boxes in the reply: the base model gave those tokens the lowest probability.

On this text GPT-2 small has a loss of 4.43 nats per question token and 4.28 per reply token, and instruction tuning counts the 25 reply tokens only.

How it works

Take the 25 reply tokens of the figure. Their mean loss is 4.28 nats, so the total that instruction tuning counts is \(25 \times 4.28 = 107\) nats. Raising \(e \approx 2.718\) to the mean loss gives the perplexity, \(e^{4.28} = 72\): a model that spread its probability evenly over 72 tokens would have this loss.

\[ L_{\text{SFT}} = -\frac{1}{|R|}\sum_{t\in R}\ln p_\theta\big(x_t \mid x_{<t}\big) \]

Here \(x_t\) is token \(t\) of the question and the reply together, \(x_{<t}\) the tokens before it, \(p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})\) the probability the model gives to \(x_t\), where \(\theta\) denotes the weights, \(R\) the set of reply positions and \(|R|\) their number, 25 here. The sum runs over \(R\), so the question positions add no term, and the division by \(|R|\) makes the loss a mean per counted token, the number the figure shows. With \(R\) as all positions the equation is the loss of pretraining.

Common belief. The model should learn from the whole text, so the question tokens should count in the loss too.

Why it fails. The user writes the question when the model is in use, and the model never has to produce it. In the figure the question tokens have a loss of 4.43 nats, so counting them would make part of the update serve the prediction of questions.

Better account. Counting only the reply is the usual setting. A team can change the setting and compare the answers the two settings give.

Quick quiz

The mean loss on a reply of 40 tokens is 3.0 nats. What is the total loss, and what is the perplexity?

The total is \(40 \times 3.0 = 120\) nats, and the perplexity is \(e^{3.0} = 20.1\).

The question tokens are left out of the loss. Does the model still read them?

Yes. They are part of the input, so they affect the probabilities of the reply tokens. They are only left out of the sum over \(R\), so the update is not driven by how well the model predicts them.

Go deeper symbols, reading the shading, a debug tip about 1 min

Symbols

  • \(x_t\) is token \(t\) of the text (question and reply together) and \(x_{<t}\) all tokens before it. \(p_\theta\) is the model's probability for the token.
  • \(R\) is the set of reply positions and \(|R|\) its size. With \(R\) as all positions this is the loss of pretraining. Here \(|R| = 25\) and the mean is 4.28, so the total is \(25 \times 4.28 = 107\) nats.

Perplexity and the shading

A token is shaded by GPT-2's loss on it (D3): a stronger colour means the base model gave it a lower probability. The specific words of the reply, such as "77", "44", "Juhu" and "rock", are among the tokens with the highest loss. Instruction tuning lowers the loss on reply tokens that follow a question. A mean loss rounded to 4.3 nats gives \(e^{4.3} \approx 74\); the unrounded 4.28 gives 72.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Mask the padding tokens as well as the question. In a batch of replies of different lengths the short ones are filled with padding (D1), and a loss that counts it teaches the model to predict padding.

Learning from preferences

Guess first. How could a model learn from only "A is better than B", when no one writes a perfect answer?

A preference pair is two replies to one question with a mark for the one people judged better. A reward model is trained on such pairs so that the preferred reply gets the higher reward score. The policy, the language model being tuned, is then adjusted to raise its expected reward score. In RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback, a penalty for moving away from the starting model limits the change. The number β, set by the slider named Leash β, is its strength: a large β pulls the policy back toward the starting model, and a small β lets it move far.

  1. With β = 1, press "Careful rater votes 10 times" three times. The left chart shows the reward scores, and the right chart the policy before (sand) and after (teal): hover the teal bar of A to see about 68%. The answers and the usefulness scores are made up.
  2. Set β = 1, press "Reset" and then "Rater who likes long answers votes 10 times" three times: hover the teal bar of D to see about 61%.
  3. Then drag "Leash β": a large β pulls the teal bars toward the sand bars.

Which answer to "How big does a grey bamboo shark grow?" is better? Click it, or let a simulated rater vote.

Reward scores learned from the votes

Policy: probability of giving an answer

At β = 1, thirty careful votes raise the made-up usefulness from 0.31 to 0.72, and thirty votes from a rater who likes long answers reach only 0.40.

How it works

Answers A and B have reward scores 1.2 and 0.2, and a rater prefers A. The sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\) turns the gap \(z = 1.0\) into the model's chance that A is preferred: \(\sigma(1.0) = 1/(1 + 0.368) = 0.731\). The loss is \(-\ln 0.731 = 0.313\). A step of size \(\eta = 0.5\) adds \(\eta(1 - 0.731) = 0.134\) to A and subtracts it from B, giving 1.334 and 0.066. The factor \(1 - 0.731\) is the loss's slope, so a vote against the scores moves them more.

\[ P(a \succ b) = \sigma\big(r_a - r_b\big) \]

Here \(P(a \succ b)\) is the model's chance that \(a\) is preferred to \(b\), and \(r_a\) is the reward score of reply \(a\). This is the Bradley-Terry model, an assumption that raters need not follow. The best trade between a high expected reward score and a small KL distance (a measure of how far the tuned policy is from the starting one) has this form: multiply the starting probability of an answer by \(e^{r/\beta}\) and rescale to add up to 1. At β = 1 the figure draws it: answers A to E with scores 1.2, 0.2, 0, 0 and −1 move from 0.22, 0.18, 0.10, 0.15 and 0.35 to A 55%, B 17%, C 8%, D 11% and E 10%. A large β keeps the multipliers near 1. Exercise 2 uses this formula and the KL distance, in Go deeper.

Common belief. Learning from human feedback teaches a model what is true.

Why it fails. A rater chooses the reply that looks better to them, so a confident, fluent reply can win over a correct reply that hedges. A reward model fitted to the votes can reproduce such habits, including a taste for length.

Better account. Preference learning moves replies toward what raters choose: style, tone, helpfulness, and correctness only where raters can tell it, so facts have to come from the pretraining text, from sources the model is given, and from checks.

Quick quiz

Equal scores: what is the first answer's chance of winning, and how far does one vote (\(\eta = 0.5\)) move the scores?

The gap is 0, so \(\sigma(0) = 0.5\). The step is \(0.5 \times (1 - 0.5) = 0.25\): the winner goes up by 0.25 and the loser down by 0.25.

What does a very large β do to the policy?

\(e^{r/\beta}\) is close to 1 for all replies, so the multipliers leave the starting probabilities almost unchanged: the policy stays near the starting model.

Go deeper policy equation, symbols, systems in use, Python about 5 min

The policy with a leash

The policy is the language model seen as probabilities over replies, and the five answers, their starting probabilities and their usefulness scores are made up for this page. The reward model sees only the votes. Worked example, the policy. Take the starting probabilities of the figure (A 0.22, B 0.18, C 0.10, D 0.15, E 0.35), the scores (1.2, 0.2, 0, 0, \(-1\)) and \(\beta = 1\). The unnormalised weights are \(0.22 e^{1.2} = 0.730\), \(0.18 e^{0.2} = 0.220\), 0.10, 0.15 and \(0.35 e^{-1} = 0.129\). They add up to 1.329, so the policy is A 55%, B 17%, C 8%, D 11% and E 10%.

\[ \pi^{*}(a) = \frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a)\,e^{\,r(a)/\beta}}{\sum_{a'}\pi_{\text{ref}}(a')\,e^{\,r(a')/\beta}},\qquad \mathrm{KL}(\pi^{*}\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}) = \sum_a \pi^{*}(a)\,\ln\frac{\pi^{*}(a)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a)} \]

The KL distance is 0 when the two policies are equal and grows as they differ. Reading the leash numbers off the figure: after 30 careful votes, hover the teal bar of A to see 38% at \(\beta = 3\) and 95% at \(\beta = 0.3\) (68% at \(\beta = 1\)).

Symbols

  • The probability \(\sigma(r_a - r_b)\) is the Bradley-Terry model (Bradley and Terry, 1952), an assumption about choices. The loss of one vote is \(\ell = -\ln\sigma(r_w - r_l)\), the log loss of A3. \(r_a\) is the reward score of reply \(a\). \(r_w\) and \(r_l\) are the scores of the chosen (winning) and the other (losing) reply. \(\sigma\) is the sigmoid.
  • The sigmoid gives 0.5 for a gap of 0, 0.731 for a gap of 1 and 0.95 for a gap of 3. The gradient of \(\ell\) with respect to the gap \(r_w - r_l\) is \(-(1 - \sigma)\). A step of size \(\eta\) therefore adds \(\eta(1-\sigma)\) to \(r_w\) and subtracts it from \(r_l\). A vote that goes against the current scores (small \(\sigma\)) moves the scores more.
  • \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) is the starting policy and \(\pi^{*}\) the policy that maximises the expected reward minus \(\beta\) times its distance (KL, B7) from \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\). As \(\beta\) grows, \(\pi^{*}\) approaches \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\). As \(\beta\) falls, \(\pi^{*}\) piles up on the best-scoring reply.

Systems in use

Systems in use differ from the toy in three ways. The reward model is a neural network that scores a whole reply. The policy is a language model with a huge space of replies, so the closed form above does not apply. Reinforcement learning takes its place, with a penalty on the distance from the starting model (Stiennon and others, 2020; Ouyang and others, 2022). Ouyang and others used the PPO algorithm for this step, with a KL penalty that is applied token by token and measured from the supervised model. Christiano and others (2017) had shown, in Atari games and simulated robot tasks, that a reward can be learned from people's comparisons of short clips. Direct preference optimization (Rafailov and others, 2023) uses the closed form to write the whole thing as a classification loss on the pairs. It needs no separate reward model and no reinforcement-learning loop.

Two cautions

Two cautions come from the figure. A reward model is a proxy for what people want, and pushing a policy hard against a proxy can lower the true quality. Gao and others (2022) measured this with a synthetic setup in which a fixed gold-standard reward model plays the part of the people. They found that optimising too hard against the proxy can lower the gold score. Singhal and others (2023) studied three settings. They found that much of the reward gain in RLHF came from longer outputs, and that a reward based on length alone recovered most of the gains. Set \(\beta\) to 0.5 and press "Rater who likes long answers votes 10 times" three times from Reset: answer D reaches 90%. The simulated votes come from a fixed random sequence that restarts at Reset, so you see the numbers of the caption. In sixteen other sequences (seeds 100 to 115 of the same random generator) the careful rater reached 0.62 to 0.76 and the rater who likes long answers 0.35 to 0.56.

In Python

import numpy as np

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

r = np.array([1.2, 0.2])                 # reward scores of answers A and B
winner, loser, eta = 0, 1, 0.5           # the rater prefers A
p = sigmoid(r[winner] - r[loser])        # model's chance that A wins
loss = -np.log(p)
r[winner] += eta * (1 - p)
r[loser] -= eta * (1 - p)
print(f"P(A beats B) = {p:.3f}, loss = {loss:.3f}, scores after the step: {r.round(3)}")

ref = np.array([0.22, 0.18, 0.10, 0.15, 0.35])    # starting policy over answers A to E (made up)
r = np.array([1.2, 0.2, 0.0, 0.0, -1.0])
for beta in (3.0, 1.0, 0.3):
    w = ref * np.exp(r / beta)
    pi = w / w.sum()
    kl = (pi * np.log(pi / ref)).sum()
    print(f"beta = {beta}: policy {pi.round(3)}, KL from the start {kl:.2f}")
P(A beats B) = 0.731, loss = 0.313, scores after the step: [1.334 0.066]
beta = 3.0: policy [0.321 0.188 0.098 0.147 0.246], KL from the start 0.04
beta = 1.0: policy [0.55  0.165 0.075 0.113 0.097], KL from the start 0.31
beta = 0.3: policy [0.951 0.028 0.008 0.012 0.001], KL from the start 1.29

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a tuned model gets wordier without getting better, compare the reward of a long and a short reply with the same content. A reward that rises with length alone is the first thing to remove.

What the model reads: prompts and templates

Guess first. A chat model reads your question and also the instruction "Answer in at most two sentences". Are the two given to the network as different inputs, or are they part of one stream of tokens?

The prompt is all the text the model reads before it writes, its context (the next-token chapter). In a chat, a chat template turns the messages of the conversation into one stream of tokens. A message starts with the special token <|im_start|> (a special token is a marker added to the text) and a role name, which says who the message is from: system, user or assistant. It ends with the special token <|im_end|>. The system prompt, instructions from the developer placed before the conversation, is ordinary text in the first message.

  1. Press "No system message": the text is 28 tokens, because the Qwen2.5-0.5B template adds a default message, "You are a helpful assistant." Pink marks are special tokens.
  2. Press "With a system message": one sentence of instructions makes it 39 tokens, in one stream where <|im_start|> and <|im_end|> mark where the messages start and end.
  3. Read the last line: the model writes its reply after <|im_start|>assistant and stops by writing <|im_end|>.

    

  
    

    
A one-line question is 28 tokens with the Qwen2.5-0.5B template, which adds a default system message, and a system message of one sentence makes it 39.

  

  

    
How it works

    
The special tokens <|im_start|> and <|im_end|> have the IDs 151644 and 151645 (the tokenisation chapter). The role name after <|im_start|> is ordinary text. When the model writes <|im_end|>, the program around the model ends the generation loop. Because the model was tuned on text in this format, the format matters: a model tuned on one template can answer badly if another is used.

    
The system prompt goes through the same network as all other text; it has no separate input, only its role name and its place first. A likely reason that replies tend to follow it is that, in the tuning data, instructions of this kind came first and the replies that followed them were the ones people wrote or preferred. Tuning does not guarantee this, so a reply can still ignore it.

    

      
Common belief. A system prompt is a rule the model must obey.

      
Why it fails. It is text in the same stream as the user's message and as any document the model reads. Tuning has made replies likely to follow it, but no mechanism forces them to, so instructions placed in a web page or a file that the model reads can compete with it.

      
Better account. The system prompt is a strong hint, learned during tuning, so rules that must always apply are enforced outside the model, in the program around it.

    

    

      
Quick quiz

      
Where does the model stop writing its reply?
When it writes the end token <|im_end|>. The program around the model watches for that token and ends the loop.

      
A web page that the model reads contains the sentence "Ignore your instructions". Why can it compete with the system prompt?
Both are ordinary text in the same stream of tokens, and no mechanism marks the system prompt as a rule that must win.

Cost of a long prompt

      
All tokens of the prompt also cost memory for the whole conversation, because their keys and values stay in the cache (D6). A system prompt of 1,000 tokens in Qwen3-4B's sizes takes \(1{,}000 \times 147{,}456\) bytes, about 147 MB.

      
About the template in the figure

      
The text is what the tokenizer of Qwen2.5-0.5B produces for the question "How big does a grey bamboo shark grow?". The instruct versions of Qwen2.5 use a longer default message ("You are Qwen, created by Alibaba Cloud. You are a helpful assistant."), so their counts differ.

      
Common mistakes

      

        
Debug tip. If a chat model behaves oddly, print the final string it received. A missing end token, a doubled system message or a different template than the model was tuned on explains many odd replies.

      

    

  







  
In-context learning

  

    
Guess first. You paste the sentence "The reef we dive on is called Velkar Ledge." above the question "What is the reef we dive on called?". Does the model's probability of "Velkar" change? Has the model learned anything?

    
In-context learning is a change in what a model does that comes from changing the prompt, with no change to its weights. In the first example below, a fact placed in the prompt raises the probability that GPT-2 small gives to the right answer. In the second, a few-shot prompt, which has a few solved examples before the new case, mostly changes the format of what GPT-2 small writes.

    

      
    
        
  1. In "Facts in the prompt", tick only the Velkar Ledge fact and choose the reef question: Vel, the first piece of the word Velkar, has 22%. Untick the fact and it falls to 0.008%. The facts are made up and the probabilities are GPT-2 small's.
    2. 
        
  2. Tick all five facts: Vel falls to 2.9%.
    3. 
        
  3. In "A rule from examples", untick all six examples: yes or no gets 0.16%. Tick them: 97.2%. Then tick "Flip all the labels" and watch how many of the six test reports get the right answer word.
    4. 
      

    

    

  
    

    
A fact in the prompt raises the first piece of the answer from 0.008% to 22%, and six solved examples raise yes or no from 0.16% to 97.2%.

  

  

    
How it works

    
The name was made up for this page, so the probability of Vel is tiny until the fact is in the prompt. The model can then copy the name from earlier text. With all five facts in the prompt, Vel falls to 2.9%, so GPT-2 small puts less probability on the right fact when it is one of five.

    
In "A rule from examples" the task is to finish a dive report with "Shark seen: yes" or "Shark seen: no", after six reports that end this way. With no example the prompt gives no sign that the answer is one of these two words, and they get 0.16%. The correct word's share of the probability on yes and no averages 53% with true answer words and 43% with all answer words flipped (yes swapped with no in the examples). Six test reports are too few to trust that gap. In the equation, \(\theta\) is the set of trained weights, the same for all prompts, \(x_1 y_1, \dots, x_k y_k\) are the \(k\) examples (a case and its answer), \(x\) is the new case and \(y\) the answer.

    
\[ p_\theta\big(y \mid x_1 y_1, \dots, x_k y_k,\; x\big) \]

    

      
Common belief. In-context learning means the model learns the rule from the examples, as it would in training.

      
Why it fails. No weight changes: \(\theta\) is the same for all prompts, so only the text before y differs, and without the prompt the effect is gone. Flipping all the answer words changed that share from 53% to 43% (six reports, so the gap is not reliable).

      
Better account. In the cases measured here, examples act mainly as context: they fix the format, the possible answer words and the kind of input in the text the model reads.

    

    

      
Quick quiz

      
After the conversation ends, does the pasted fact still change the answers?
No. The fact was only in the prompt, so its keys and values were in the cache for that conversation. The weights did not change.

      
What did six solved examples show GPT-2 small most clearly?
The format: the answer is the word yes or no. The probability on those two words went from 0.16% to 97.2%. The choice between them improved only a little.

    

  

  

    Go deeper induction heads, other studies, symbols, a debug tip about 2 min
    


Induction heads and the first view

      
Copying from earlier text is what induction heads do: attention heads that find an earlier copy of the current token and copy what came next (D4).

      
More on the first view

      
With all five facts in the prompt the probability of Vel falls to 2.9%: GPT-2 small, a small model with 124 million weights, puts less probability on the right fact when it is one of five.

      
Induction heads

      
Olsson and others (2022) report evidence that induction heads may drive most in-context learning in large transformers, causal evidence in small attention-only models and correlational evidence in larger ones. D4 found the head L5H5 of GPT-2 doing this on a repeated tag number.

      
More on the second view

      
With true answer words GPT-2 small gives the correct word the higher probability for 4 of the 6 test reports, and with all answer words flipped for 2 of 6. The correct word's share of the probability on yes and no averages 53% with true answer words, a little above a coin toss, and 43% with flipped ones. Six test reports are too few to trust the ten-point gap. With no example, yes or no gets 0.16% in the figure, about 0.2%.

      
What other studies found

      
Min and others (2022) tested 12 models, including GPT-3, and found that replacing the labels of the examples at random barely hurt classification and multiple-choice tasks. They conclude that the examples help by showing the label space, the kind of input and the format. Larger models may use the pairing of input and label more, which has to be measured for the task. Brown and others (2020) showed with GPT-3 that few-shot performance, with no gradient update, improves with the size of the model.

      
Symbols

      
    
        
  • \(\theta\) is the set of trained weights, the same in all prompts. \(x_1 y_1, \dots, x_k y_k\) are the \(k\) examples in the prompt, and \(x\) is the new case. Only the text before \(y\) changes.
    • 
        
  • The examples are read by attention (D4). Their keys and values are kept in the cache of D5 for as long as they are in the prompt, and they cost context (D6).
    •

All numbers are next-token probabilities from GPT-2 small, computed offline for all choices of prompt. The facts and the reports are made up.

      
Common mistakes

      

        
Debug tip. Keep the examples in one identical format, including spaces and line breaks, and end the prompt where the answer should begin. In the second view all examples end with " Shark seen: yes" or " Shark seen: no". The new report ends with " Shark seen:", so the next token is the label.

      

    

  







  
Tools and skills

  

    
Guess first. A model cannot read your catch table and cannot do long arithmetic reliably. What could it do instead of guessing, if it were allowed to ask for help?

    
A tool is a function that the program around the model, the application, can run for it. A model with tools only produces text. It writes a tool call, which is text that names the tool and its arguments, the application runs the function, and the result returns to the model as more text.

    

      
    
        
  1. Choose "Mean length of bamboo sharks?" and press "Next step": the grey text was already there and the green part is new. The text is the Qwen2.5 template with tools. The model's lines are scripted for this page, and the tool runs on the made-up catch table and dive log in your browser.
    2. 
        
  2. Press "Reset", choose "The model misspells the species", and press "Next step": the error returns as text, and the model writes the call again.
    3. 
      

    

    

    

    

  
    

    
The model only writes text, a program runs the tool, and the result is added to the text before the model writes its answer.

  

  

    
How it works

    
The application first builds the text that the model reads: the system message, the definitions of three tools (about 327 tokens in this template) and the question. Next the model writes a tool call for mean_length with the species bamboo, and stops. It hands over only its text: the application reads the model's text, finds the call and runs the function on the made-up catch table. The application adds the result, 47.4 cm (72 records), to the text, and the model then writes an answer that uses it.

    
A skill is a folder with a file SKILL.md that has a name, a description and the instructions. In the documentation of Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, the name and description of a skill are in the text from the start, about 100 tokens per skill. The model reads the descriptions and itself asks for the body of SKILL.md, under 5,000 tokens, when a request matches one, so only the descriptions are always in the text.

    

      
    
        
  1. Press "Message 1", "Message 2" and "Message 3": the top bar (names and descriptions) is always there, and the middle bar is the SKILL.md of the skill that the message matches, except for Message 3, where no skill matches. Extra files stay at zero until the instructions point to them.
    2. 
      

    

    
    

  
    

    

      
Common belief. A model with tools can check its own answers, so it cannot make things up.

      
Why it fails. It may skip the tool, call it with the wrong arguments, misread the result or trust a wrong source. The reply after the tool result is still written one token at a time, so it can differ from the result.

      
Better account. A tool puts facts from a source into the text, so the answer need not rely on the weights for those facts; this can lower made-up answers on them. It does not remove them. The transcript of calls and results is what you check.

    

    

      
Quick quiz

      
Who runs the tool, the model or the application?
The application. The model writes the call as text. The application reads it, runs the function and adds the result to the text.

      
Why can many skills be installed without filling the context?
Only the name and description of a skill, about 100 tokens, are always in the context. The body and the extra files are read only when a request needs them.

    

  

  

    Go deeper the API, training, Socratic Tutor, Python about 4 min
    


The same loop in the Anthropic API

      
The tool definitions are text too, and they are read again with all requests. In the Anthropic API the loop appears as a stop reason tool_use with a block that names the tool and its arguments. Your code runs the operation and sends back a tool_result, and the model then writes the reply (Anthropic documentation, opened for this chapter). In the figure, "The model misspells the species" makes the tool return an error as text, and the model, which reads it, writes the call again. An application should also limit the number of rounds, so that a confused model cannot loop.

      
How models are trained to call tools

      
Toolformer (Schick and others, 2023) trains a model so that its text includes calls to tools, with the choice of tool, the place of the call and its arguments learned from a few examples per tool. ReAct (Yao and others, 2022) has the model write a short thought before an action. On two question-answering tasks it reduced hallucination compared with reasoning alone, by their report, which they attribute to the facts coming from a source and not from the weights.

      
Skills in three levels

      
The documentation of Anthropic describes three levels. Claude sees the name and description of a skill at the start, about 100 tokens per skill. When a request matches a description, Claude reads the body of SKILL.md, under 5,000 tokens. Extra files are read only when the instructions point to them, and a script's code never enters the context, only its output.

      
About the skills figure

      
The sizes are the typical values stated in the documentation, drawn to one scale. The messages and the matching follow the test cases of the Socratic Tutor, where the model reads the descriptions and itself calls for the skill that matches.

      
Bridge to the Socratic Tutor



    
Bridge to our Socratic Tutor. The Socratic Tutor of Mumbai AI Lab is a plugin that makes Claude tutor by asking questions. It has two skills, socratic-tutor and quiz-me, and no code, only written instructions. The report explains how a Claude plugin works and when a skill loads. It sets out the rules of the tutor and the studies behind them. The rules are one question per turn, a ladder of questions, a hint scale, and a rule for when it gives the answer. It works through the mechanism of this chapter: instructions added to the context, not a change of weights. The same text could be a system prompt. The skill form keeps it out of the context until a request needs it.

  

      
In Python


import json, numpy as np

# the made-up catch table of the running example (records are rows of the table)
catch = json.load(open("catch.json"))["records"]

def mean_length(species):
    rows = [r["length_cm"] for r in catch if r["species"] == species]
    if not rows:
        return f'error: unknown species "{species}"'
    return f"{np.mean(rows):.1f} cm ({len(rows)} records)"

TOOLS = {"mean_length": mean_length}

def scripted_model(messages):
    """A scripted replacement for the language model: it only ever returns text."""
    last = messages[-1]
    if last["role"] == "user":
        return 'CALL mean_length("bamboos")'               # a misspelling, on purpose
    if last["content"].startswith("error"):
        return 'CALL mean_length("bamboo")'
    return "The bamboo sharks in the made-up table have a mean length of " + last["content"].split(" cm")[0] + " cm."

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the mean length of the bamboo sharks?"}]
for step in range(5):                                       # a limit, so a confused model cannot loop forever
    reply = scripted_model(messages)
    print("model  :", reply)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
    if not reply.startswith("CALL "):
        break
    name, arg = reply[5:].split("(")
    result = TOOLS[name](arg.strip(')"'))
    print("tool   :", result)
    messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": result})


model  : CALL mean_length("bamboos")
tool   : error: unknown species "bamboos"
model  : CALL mean_length("bamboo")
tool   : 47.4 cm (72 records)
model  : The bamboo sharks in the made-up table have a mean length of 47.4 cm.

      
Common mistakes

      

        
Debug tip. When an answer from a tool-using model is wrong, read the transcript in three places. Was the call right? What did the tool return? Did the answer use the returned text?

      

    

  







  
Why a model makes things up

  

    
Guess first. GPT-2 reads "The Ganges shark was recorded at Sassoon Dock in Mumbai in the year", and the true year is 2016. Does it put most of its probability on 2016, on a few years near it, or on a wide spread? And what does it do if the animal does not exist?

    
A model must give a probability to some next token. A hallucination is a fluent statement that is false or has no support in the input or the data. When the true answer is rare in the training text, plausible wrong tokens can take most of the probability, so a fluent false sentence follows. Temperature T is a sampling setting: a lower T gives the most likely token a larger share, and a higher T spreads probability more evenly.

    

      
    
        
  1. Press "A fact in many texts": 67% goes to the true token, Maharashtra (teal). Coral marks a false or unsupported token of the right kind, and sand any other token.
    2. 
        
  2. Press "A true fact few texts state", then "Draw 200 continuations": the line under the chart counts how many are true, answer-like but false, or other. Drag "Temperature T" and draw again to compare. The true year is 2016.
    3. 
        
  3. In the last two views the species is made up for this page, so no token is true.
    4. 
      

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

  
    

    
For a fact in many texts GPT-2 small puts 67% on the true token, but only 2.2% for a true fact the page takes to be rarer, with 75% on other years.

  

  

    
How it works

    
In the year context the model gives 17% to the false year 2000 and 2.2% to the true year, 2016, so the greedy choice (the most likely token) is a false year. A state name and a year differ in more than how often the fact is stated, so the two contexts show a pattern and cannot show its cause. The entropy H measures how far probability is spread, and \(e^{H}\) (with \(e \approx 2.718\)) is the number of equally likely tokens that would give the same \(H\): four equally likely tokens give \(H = \ln 4 = 1.39\) and \(e^{H} = 4\). Here \(H = 4.58\) nats (4.577 before rounding) gives \(e^{H} = 97\) effective choices, and a uniform choice among 97 tokens would give the true year \(1/97 = 1.0\%\), so the model's 2.2% is only about twice that.

    
\[ H = -\sum_k p_k \ln p_k,\qquad \text{effective choices} = e^{H} \]

    
Here \(p_k\) is the probability of token \(k\). For the species that does not exist no token is true. Yet 61% of the probability goes to numbers when the text asks for a length, and 18% to tokens that begin a person's name when it asks for a name. The text gives no sign that the species is missing.

    

      
Common belief. A model that states something false is lying, or knows the truth and hides it.

      
Why it fails. The model computes probabilities over next tokens, and false tokens that fit the sentence take a share, as the true year's 2.2% shows. No part of this computation looks the claim up in a source.

      
Better account. The model produces a likely continuation. Whether it is true depends on the training data and the tuning, and checking decides whether the error is caught.

    

    

      
Quick quiz

      
Why does GPT-2 answer a question about a species that does not exist?
A model must give a probability to some next token, and a question about a species is followed in text by an answer-like token such as a number. The text gives no sign that the species is missing.

      
Does a lower temperature remove hallucination?
No. A lower temperature gives the most likely token a larger share. In the year context the most likely token is a false year, so a lower temperature makes the false year more certain.

    

  

  

    Go deeper four causes, what helps, symbols about 4 min
    


More on the views

      
In the first view, "Mumbai is the capital of the Indian state of", the model puts 67% on Maharashtra and 13% on Gujarat, and the effective number of choices is 4 (the entropy of D3). In the year context the model spreads its probability over years: 2000 at 17%, then 2010, 2015 and 2013 at 2 to 3%, and the true year has rank 9. It gives 16.7% to the year 2000, which is wrong, and 2.2% to the true year, about twice the 1.0% of a uniform choice among its 97 effective choices. The model has learned something, and that is too little to answer. In the fourth view the tokens that begin a person's name include Dr, William and Charles, and there are about 1,050 effective choices.

      
GPT-2 small is a small model. A larger one stores more facts in its weights and would probably give the true year more weight, but it also has facts it saw once or never, and the same thing happens there.

      
Four causes

      
Four causes appear in the research. They combine.

      
    
        
  • The objective. The objective of pretraining is high probability for the observed next token (D3). The softmax gives all tokens a probability, and the model has no way to abstain unless the training text contained abstaining in that place. "I do not know" is a continuation that has to be learned.
    • 
        
  • Rare facts. Kalai and Vempala (2023) prove a bound for facts that cannot be inferred from other training data. A calibrated model, one whose confidence matches how often it is right, must hallucinate on them at a rate of at least about the share of facts that appear once only in training, the singletons. Their bound applies even with error-free data and is not caused by the transformer architecture. Facts seen many times, and systematic facts such as arithmetic, do not face the same necessity.
    • 
        
  • Scoring that rewards guessing. Kalai, Nachum, Vempala and Zhang (2025) argue that hallucinations begin as errors in telling valid from invalid statements, and stay because most tests are graded so that guessing pays. They propose changing how existing tests are scored.
    • 
        
  • Tuning toward answers. The tuned model is trained on replies that answer, and a reward model that scores confident, helpful replies higher pushes the tuned model in the same direction. This is a plausible account, and this page does not measure it. The third stage of the first figure shows an admission of ignorance, which appears only if the training data and the preferences contain it.
    • 
      

      
What helps

      
Several measures help. One is grounding, which is tying an answer to a source that the model is given or can look up. Putting the facts in the prompt is a form of it: in the first view of the last section the probability of the right token rose from 0.008% to 22%. Tools that fetch a source help too, since ReAct reduced hallucination in two question-answering tasks, by its authors' report. Asking for the source and checking it also helps, and so does scoring tests so that a wrong answer costs more than an abstention. These measures reduce made-up answers and do not remove them.

      
Symbols

      
\[ \text{rate of hallucination} \gtrsim s \]

      
    
        
  • \(p_k\) is the probability of next token \(k\) (D3). \(e^{H}\) is the number of equally likely tokens that would give the same entropy: 4 for the Maharashtra context and 97 for the year context.
    • 
        
  • \(s\) is the share of the training facts that appear once only, the singleton rate. The bound of Kalai and Vempala applies to facts that cannot be inferred from other data, and it ignores smaller terms (written \(\gtrsim\)).
    • 
      

      
Common mistakes

      

        
Debug tip. Ask the same question several times at a temperature above zero. Answers that change show that the probability is spread over several answers. Answers that repeat do not show truth: the greedy choice for the year context is the false year 2000 in all runs.

  1. theory Two answers have scores \(r_a = 0.4\) and \(r_b = -0.2\). What is \(P(a \succ b)\)? What is the loss if a rater prefers \(a\), and what if the rater prefers \(b\)? How far does either outcome move the scores for \(\eta = 0.5\)?

    \(P = \sigma(0.6)\). The loss is \(-\ln\) of the probability of the outcome that happened. The step is \(\eta\) times (1 minus that probability).

Come back later

  

    
(D3) Why does greedy decoding sometimes repeat a sentence, as GPT-2 did in the first figure?
Greedy decoding picks the most likely token at a step. Once a sentence is written, the most likely continuation of the text is often to write it again, so the loop repeats.

    
(B7, D6) Instruction tuning changes weights, and in-context learning does not. Which of the two is test-time training closer to, and what is the difference?
Test-time training changes weights, like tuning, but only fast weights, for one input, and they go back to the trained values for the next input. In-context learning changes only the prompt.

    
(D5, D6) A system prompt of 1,000 tokens is added to all conversations with Qwen3-4B. How much cache does it use in 16-bit numbers?
Qwen3-4B needs 147,456 bytes of cache per token, so \(1{,}000 \times 147{,}456 = 147\) MB, as long as the conversation lasts.
